theme: Vows and devoted things, the conclusion
readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 27:1-34. This is the last chapter of Leviticus, and it deals with vows and gifts to the sanctuary. It may seem like an odd ending, so read it as a final lesson about what it means to belong to God.
settingTheScene: After the great statements of covenant blessing and curse in chapter 26, the book ends with an appendix about vows. A person might promise himself, his family members, his animals, his house, or his land to the LORD. This chapter explains how to value those promises and how to redeem them. It closes the book with a practical reminder that gifts to God are real, and should be taken seriously.
observation: The chapter begins with “When a man makes a special vow to the LORD involving the valuation of persons” (27:2).
A person’s value is set in shekels according to age and sex (27:3-7).
The poor could be valued according to what they were able to pay (27:8).
A person who dedicates an animal cannot substitute a better or worse one (27:10).
Someone who wants to redeem a house or field must add a fifth to its value (27:13, 15, 19).
The firstborn of animals already belongs to the LORD and cannot be vowed (27:26).
“Every devoted thing is most holy to the LORD” (27:28).

“All the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD’s; it is holy to the LORD” (27:30). The book ends: “These are the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses for the people of Israel on Mount Sinai” (27:34).
interpretation:
The last chapter of Leviticus may seem like an anticlimax, but it ties a few themes together.

The first is the seriousness of promises to God. A vow was voluntary, but once made, it was binding. The chapter provides a way to redeem what was promised, but at a cost. The lesson is that words matter. When you make a promise to God, it is not a casual matter. Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 will say the same: “It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay.”

The second is that everything belongs to God. The firstborn animals are the LORD’s already. The tithe is the LORD’s. The land is the LORD’s, as chapter 25 said. Even the idea of giving something to God is a recognition that he owns it all. When you give, you are not paying God. You are acknowledging what is already his.

The third is the matter of valuation. The chapter assigns a price to persons, and that sounds strange to modern ears. It is not a statement of a person’s worth. It is the amount required to redeem a person who was dedicated to the sanctuary. Without it, someone dedicated to the LORD would have no way back to normal life.

Look at the larger shape of the book. Leviticus begins with the call from the tent of meeting, and the first words are, “If anyone of you brings an offering to the LORD.” It ends with the tithe and the devoted things. The book began with the offering and ends with the offerer. It shows what a holy people look like: they have been redeemed, they have been cleansed, and they give themselves to God.

The final verse is a reminder of where all this began. These commandments came on Mount Sinai. The book is not a collection of legal puzzles. It is the voice of the God who rescued Israel, speaking to the people he lives among.
connection: Jesus praised the widow who gave two small coins, because she gave “all she had to live on” (Mark 12:41-44). Paul urges Christians to give “not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Peter says that you were redeemed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold” but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19). The price that redeems you is not a figure on a chart. It is the life of the Son.
application:
Think about any promise you have made to God that you have not kept. Bring it to him honestly.

Ask whether you treat what you have as yours or as his. Choose one concrete act of giving this week.

Thank God that the cost of your redemption has been paid by Christ.
prayerPrompts: Give God what is already his, and tell him what you want to give.
Confess promises you have not kept.
Thank him for the price paid for you in Jesus’ blood.
